t: The cervix, HPV and cervical cancer screening
sub: Why cervical cancer starts in the transformation zone, how HPV E6 and E7 drive it, and how screening catches it early.

pretest.q: Which HPV protein inactivates the retinoblastoma (Rb) protein?
pretest.why: E7 binds Rb and releases the E2F transcription factors, so the cell moves from G1 into S phase without its normal checkpoint. E6 is the partner protein that destroys p53.

w.E6: E6 attacks the other brake. It targets p53 for destruction, so damaged cells skip arrest and apoptosis.
w.L1: L1 is the major capsid protein that forms the viral shell. The vaccine uses it to make virus-like particles, and it has no role in the cell cycle.
w.E2: E2 is the viral gene that normally keeps E6 and E7 low. Integration breaks it, which raises oncoprotein levels, but E2 does not bind Rb.

pretest.q: Where on the cervix does squamous metaplasia create the cells that high-risk HPV transforms?
pretest.why: Estrogen everts columnar epithelium onto the ectocervix, and the acidic vagina turns it squamous. The immature metaplastic cells of this transformation zone are the ones HPV infects and transforms.

w.Internal os: The internal os is where the endocervical canal meets the uterine cavity. It is lined by glandular cells and is not the usual site of squamous neoplasia.
w.Mid-portion of the ectocervix: The outer ectocervix has mature, glycogen-rich squamous epithelium that finished metaplasia long ago, so it is far less vulnerable to viral transformation.
w.Vaginal fornix: The fornix is lined by vaginal squamous epithelium. Vaginal cancers are rare and usually spread from the cervix rather than starting there.

pretest.q: A 22-year-old on a combined oral contraceptive has mucoid discharge and spotting after intercourse. The cervix shows a red ring around the os, and cytology is normal. What explains this?
pretest.why: Estrogen everts the columnar endocervical lining onto the ectocervix, where its fragile cells make mucus and bleed on contact. Ectropion is benign and common with oral contraceptives, adolescence and pregnancy.

w.Invasive squamous cell carcinoma: Invasive cancer presents as a friable, ulcerated or exophytic mass with abnormal cytology or biopsy. A smooth red ring with a normal Pap points to benign ectropion.
w.Nabothian cyst: A nabothian cyst is a smooth, mucus-filled dome from a blocked gland. It does not cause discharge or bleeding, and it does not look like a red ring around the os.
w.Cervical stenosis: Stenosis narrows the opening after excision, radiation or atrophy and traps menstrual blood, causing cyclic pain or hematometra rather than a red, bleeding ring.

body: Why does cervical cancer start in the transformation zone?

The cervix is lined by two kinds of epithelium. The **ectocervix**, the part visible from the vagina, has tough nonkeratinized squamous epithelium, like the vagina itself. The endocervix, the canal behind it, has mucus-secreting columnar cells. At puberty, estrogen pushes the columnar lining outward onto the ectocervix. The acidic vagina irritates it, and it changes into squamous epithelium by **metaplasia**. The band where this happens, between the original and the new squamocolumnar junction, is the {{rp13_tz|transformation zone}}. Its immature cells are exactly the cells that high-risk HPV infects.

A Pap smear is reliable only if it samples this zone. The clinician scrapes the ectocervix with a spatula and the canal with a brush. A sample with no endocervical or metaplastic cells may have missed the zone, so even a negative result is less reassuring. Sometimes metaplastic epithelium covers the opening of an endocervical gland and traps its mucus. This forms a {{rp13_nabothian|nabothian cyst}}, a smooth, harmless bump that needs no treatment.
After menopause the junction hides in the canal

Low estrogen makes the squamocolumnar junction retreat up the endocervical canal, out of reach of a spatula. A brush is then needed to sample the **transformation zone**. If {{rp13_colpo|colposcopy}}, a magnified look at the cervix, cannot see the whole junction, it is inadequate. **Endocervical curettage** then scrapes the canal to sample the hidden part.
What happens when the cervix is everted or scarred?

When estrogen is high, as in adolescence, pregnancy or oral contraceptive use, a large area of columnar epithelium shows on the ectocervix. This red, velvety ring around the opening is called {{rp13_ectropion|ectropion}}. The fragile columnar cells make extra mucus and bleed easily, so the patient notices mucoid discharge and spotting after intercourse. Ectropion is benign, but contact bleeding still needs a Pap test to exclude cervicitis and cancer.

Scarring does the opposite. After excision of the zone, radiation or severe inflammation, the opening can narrow (**cervical stenosis**). Menstrual blood then collects in the uterus as **hematometra**, causing cyclic pain and an enlarged uterus without visible bleeding.
How does high-risk HPV turn a cervical cell into a cancer cell?

Human papillomavirus (HPV) is a nonenveloped DNA virus that enters basal cells through tiny breaks in the epithelium. Types 6 and 11 are low risk and cause genital warts. **High-risk** types, mainly 16 and then 18, cause most cervical cancers. The immune system clears most infections within one to two years, so cancer needs a **persistent** infection. In a persistent infection the viral DNA can integrate into the host genome. Integration usually breaks the viral E2 gene, which normally keeps the oncogenes E6 and E7 quiet. Freed from that brake, E6 and E7 are made in excess and switch off two tumor suppressors.
p53, which is sent to the proteasome and destroyed
No G1 arrest or apoptosis after DNA damage, so mutations pile up
Rb, which is inactivated so that E2F is released
The G1 checkpoint is lost, so cells enter S phase freely and p16 builds up
E6 destroys p53; E7 disables Rb

Remember E6 as the p53 destroyer and E7 as the Rb disabler. Working Rb normally keeps p16 low, so when E7 inactivates Rb, p16 piles up. Diffuse, block-like {{rp13_p16|p16 staining}} therefore marks a lesion driven by high-risk HPV.
How do CIN grades map onto LSIL and HSIL?

**Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN)** describes how much of the epithelium is replaced by atypical cells, which begin in the basal layer. In CIN 1 the atypical cells fill the lower third of the epithelium. In CIN 2 they fill the lower two-thirds. In CIN 3 they fill more than two-thirds, up to the full thickness (carcinoma in situ). The basement membrane stays intact at every grade, so CIN cannot metastasize. In the two-tier system, CIN 1 is **LSIL** (low grade) and CIN 2 or 3 is **HSIL** (high grade).

{{rp13_koil|Koilocytes}} show HPV's effect on a cell. They are squamous cells with an enlarged, dark, wrinkled (raisinoid) nucleus and a clear halo around it, and they are typical of LSIL. CIN 1 usually regresses because the immune system clears the virus, whereas CIN 3 tends to progress to cancer. When a lesion looks like CIN 2, diffuse p16 staining supports calling it HSIL.

On a Pap smear, LSIL cells are large, mature cells with plenty of cytoplasm and a mildly enlarged nucleus. HSIL cells are smaller and immature, so the dark, irregular nucleus fills most of the cell (a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio). Pap results use the {{rp13_bethesda|Bethesda System}}. The main categories are negative (NILM), ASC-US, LSIL, HSIL and atypical glandular cells. ASC-US, atypical squamous cells of uncertain significance, is the most common abnormal result. Atypical glandular cells come from the endocervix or endometrium.
From HPV infection to invasive carcinoma
HPV enters immature basal cells, and most women clear it within two years.
If infection persists (HPV 16, smoking, immunosuppression), the viral DNA integrates into host DNA.
p53 and Rb stop working and mutations pile up, producing CIN 2 and CIN 3.
Cells invade the stroma and HSIL becomes carcinoma, usually after many years. This is why screening every few years works.
Who is screened, with which test, and how often?

Screening looks for precancer in women without symptoms. It works because HPV lesions progress slowly, so a test every few years catches them before they invade. Under USPSTF guidance (as of 2025), screening starts at age 21, whatever the sexual history. Women aged 21 to 29 get **cytology** alone. HPV infection is very common and usually temporary at this age, so HPV testing would flag many infections that would clear anyway. After age 30 a persistent infection is more likely to matter, so HPV testing is added.
Primary HPV test, or a **cotest** (cytology plus HPV test)
Stop if recent screening was adequate and negative
After total hysterectomy for benign disease
Screen more often, and continue for life
Why can HPV testing be spaced every 5 years when cytology alone needs every 3 years?

A negative HPV test means no high-risk virus is present. Without the virus a precancer cannot develop, so the risk over the next five years is very low. Cytology is a single look at cells and misses some lesions, so a negative result is less reassuring and is repeated sooner. Because progression to invasive cancer takes many years, either schedule still catches lesions before they invade.
What happens after an abnormal screening result?

HPV vaccination is **primary prevention**, because it stops infection. Screening is **secondary prevention**, because it finds precancer early enough to remove. A screening test only sorts patients by risk and never gives a diagnosis. An abnormal result leads to colposcopy, in which the cervix is magnified after acetic acid is applied. Abnormal areas turn white and are biopsied, and the biopsy gives the diagnosis. For ASC-US, the mildest abnormal result, a reflex HPV test on the same sample sorts the risk, and a positive test goes on to colposcopy.

Treatment follows the biopsy grade. CIN 1 is usually watched with repeat testing, because most cases regress. High-grade lesions (CIN 2 or 3) are removed by excising the transformation zone. A {{rp13_leep|loop electrosurgical excision procedure}} (LEEP) uses a thin wire loop with electric current, in the office under local anesthesia. A cone biopsy cuts out a cone of tissue with a scalpel in the operating room. Both give a specimen for the pathologist to check margins and invasion.
Excision treats precancer but can weaken the cervix

Removing a cone of cervical tissue treats HSIL, but the shorter, weaker cervix may open painlessly in a later pregnancy. This **cervical insufficiency** causes second-trimester loss or **preterm** birth. For this reason excision is kept for high-grade lesions, and low-grade lesions are only watched.
Why does dysplastic epithelium turn white when acetic acid is applied at colposcopy?

Acetic acid clumps nuclear proteins. Normal mature squamous cells are mostly cytoplasm, so light passes through to the red tissue below and the surface looks pink. Dysplastic cells have large nuclei and little cytoplasm, so the clumped protein reflects light and the area turns white. The whitening follows nuclear density, so it points to the worst area to biopsy.
How does invasive cervical cancer present, and how does it kill?

About three-quarters of invasive cervical cancers are **squamous cell carcinoma**. Adenocarcinoma, from the glands of the endocervix, is second and is more closely linked to HPV 18. It starts higher in the canal, where cytology samples it less reliably, so screening has lowered its incidence less than that of squamous carcinoma. Under the microscope, squamous carcinoma forms irregular nests of atypical cells that have broken through the basement membrane, and well-differentiated tumors make keratin pearls and show intercellular bridges.

Worldwide, cervical cancer is the most common gynecologic cancer, because many women lack screening and HPV vaccination. In the United States it is the least common of the three main gynecologic cancers, and it is diagnosed at a younger age than endometrial or ovarian cancer, most often between 35 and 44. Risk factors reflect HPV exposure and persistence: early first intercourse, many partners, smoking, immunosuppression such as HIV, and poor screening. Early cancers cause no symptoms and are found only by screening. Larger tumors cause bleeding after intercourse (**postcoital** bleeding), irregular bleeding and a watery, blood-tinged discharge. The tumor spreads directly into the tissue beside the cervix and compresses the ureters. The resulting bilateral **hydronephrosis** and renal failure are a leading cause of death.
How do vaccination, HIV and cervicitis change the plan?

The HPV **vaccine** is made of recombinant L1 capsid protein, which assembles into empty virus-like particles. It has no viral DNA, so it cannot cause infection. The 9-valent vaccine covers types 6 and 11 (warts), 16 and 18 (the main cancer types), and five other high-risk types. As of 2025 it is given routinely at age 11 to 12, with catch-up through age 26. Vaccinated women are still screened on the usual schedule, because the vaccine does not cover every cancer-causing type and does not clear an existing infection.

HIV changes the timeline because immunosuppression lets HPV persist. The lower the **CD4** count, the worse the clearance of HPV and the higher the rates of CIN and cancer. Invasive cervical cancer is therefore an AIDS-defining illness, and women with HIV are screened more often. HPV also infects the anus, which has its own transformation zone, so people with HIV get more **anal cancer**. They are screened with anal cytology, and an abnormal result leads to anoscopy with biopsy.

**Cervicitis** is a different problem. It causes a mucopurulent endocervical discharge and a friable cervix that bleeds when swabbed. Chlamydia and gonorrhea are the most common causes found, so nucleic acid amplification testing looks for both, although often no organism is identified. When either is found, the patient and her partners are treated, because the infection can ascend to cause pelvic inflammatory disease.

body.q: A 60-year-old's colposcopy cannot show the whole squamocolumnar junction. Which reasoning best explains the next step?
o: Low estrogen has pulled the junction up into the canal, so the hidden zone must be sampled by endocervical curettage
The junction has spread outward across the ectocervix, so a wider ectocervical biopsy will capture the zone
Low estrogen has made the transformation zone disappear, so no further cervical sampling is needed
Chronic inflammation has hidden the junction, so treating cervicitis first will bring the zone back into view
body.why: After menopause the cervix shrinks and the junction retreats into the endocervical canal. The transformation zone still exists and is still where HPV lesions arise, but it is out of sight, so colposcopy is inadequate. Endocervical curettage samples the canal where the zone now lies. Biopsy of the visible ectocervix samples mature squamous cells that are rarely the problem, and inflammation does not move the junction.

grid.q: Which of these raise the risk of cervical cancer?
items: HIV infection with a low CD4 count
